etymology: A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name is taken to mean “a man’s wall” or “God separates.”
biblical_def: Kithlish is a city in the lowland of Judah, named once in the roll of Judah’s inheritance: “And Cabbon, and Lahmam, and Kithlish” (Jos 15:40). It is among the last towns of a Shephelah cluster and is nowhere else mentioned. The name is taken by some to carry the sense of separation — that God divides and sets apart. However uncertain the etymology, the truth of separation runs through the whole story of the inheritance, for the LORD had separated Israel from the peoples to be a possession unto Himself, and had separated the towns of Canaan from the hand of the Amorite to give them to His people. Every name in this catalogue is a boundary-stone of that separation: this town, and not the Philistine’s; this field, given to Judah, and not left to the heathen. “The LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself” (Psa 4:3). What God did in the map of Canaan He does in redemption: He separates a people to Himself out of the mass of fallen mankind, marking them off by sovereign grace, and settling them at last in an inheritance incorruptible. Little Kithlish, of which the world knows nothing, was Judah’s by the LORD’s dividing hand; and every soul chosen in Christ is His by the same electing separation, kept for a possession that fadeth not away.

etymology: A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah; also the name King Amaziah gave to the rock-city Selah of Edom after he took it. The name is taken to mean “subdued by God” or “the blessedness of God.”
biblical_def: Joktheel is a city in the lowland of Judah, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance: “And Dilean, and Mizpeh, and Joktheel” (Jos 15:38). The same name meets us again in a striking act of King Amaziah of Judah, who “slew of Edom in the valley of salt ten thousand, and took Selah by war, and called the name of it Joktheel unto this day” (2Ki 14:7). The name is taken to mean subdued by God, and Amaziah’s renaming of the Edomite stronghold declares the confession that it was God who subdued it — the victory was the LORD’s, not the arm of the king. Yet the history warns as loudly as it teaches. This same Amaziah, flushed with the conquest, carried home the gods of Edom and bowed himself before them, and his end was ruin and a conspirator’s sword. To name a fortress “subdued by God” and then worship the gods of the subdued is the height of folly and ingratitude. The lesson of Joktheel is that every victory the believer wins is God’s subduing, and must be answered not with pride nor with borrowed idols, but with worship of the LORD alone who gave it. The name preaches; the man’s later apostasy is the counter-sermon.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of the tribe of Simeon, within the territory of Judah; called Bethuel by the Chronicler and Chesil in the parallel Judah list. The name is taken to mean “dweller in God” or “man of God.”
biblical_def: Bethul is a city given to the tribe of Simeon, whose portion lay within the borders of Judah in the dry south country: “And Eltolad, and Bethul, and Hormah” (Jos 19:4). The Chronicler names the same town Bethuel (1Ch 4:30), and it appears as Chesil in the parallel Judah list (Jos 15:30). The name is taken to mean dweller in God, or man of God. This is fitting for a town of Simeon, for Simeon had no separate country but dwelt scattered in the midst of Judah, his inheritance swallowed up in his brother’s — a living fulfilment of Jacob’s dying word: “I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” (Gen 49:7). What was spoken over Simeon and Levi as a chastening for their fierce anger became, in Levi’s case, a means of blessing, as the priests were scattered to teach; and Simeon too was preserved, not blotted out, dwelling among his brethren. A town called “dweller in God” set in this scattered inheritance quietly preaches that the true dwelling-place of God’s people is not a plot of ground but the LORD Himself: “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psa 90:1). Simeon’s scattering could not rob him of the only home that finally matters — the God who is Himself the habitation of His people.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of Simeon, in the south country; called Hazar-susim by the Chronicler. The name means “village of horses” or “the horse-station.”
biblical_def: Hazar-susah is a city given to the tribe of Simeon in the dry south of Judah: “And Ziklag, and Bethmarcaboth, and Hazarsusah” (Jos 19:5). The Chronicler names it Hazar-susim (1Ch 4:31). The name means village of horses, and it likely marked a station on the caravan and chariot routes of the Negeb, perhaps a place where horses were kept for the traffic of the south. There is a quiet irony in a horse-town belonging to Israel, for the horse in Scripture stands as the great emblem of trust in military might, and the LORD forbade His kings to multiply horses (Deu 17:16) and warned His people against leaning upon them. “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The prophet cries woe upon those who “go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many…but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 31:1). So the village of horses becomes a preached warning set within the inheritance itself: the strength of a horse is nothing before God, and the people who possess horse-towns must never make horses their hope. Salvation belongs to the LORD, and the battle is His; the horse is a vain thing for safety, and cannot deliver by his great strength.
webster_summary: A city of Simeon whose name means “village of horses”; a standing warning against the trust in cavalry and might that Scripture answers with trust in the LORD.

The chariot is only newer in our day — the missile, the market, the machine — but the idolatry is the same, to lean on the arm of flesh.

Scripture answers with the fear of the LORD. “An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength” (Psa 33:17). The king was forbidden to multiply horses; the people were warned not to go down to Egypt for help. The believer remembers the name of the LORD his God, and reckons that safety, victory, and deliverance are His alone to give, whatever the count of the horses.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of Simeon, in the south country of Judah; the name is taken to mean “gracious dwelling” or “abode of grace.”
biblical_def: Sharuhen is a city given to the tribe of Simeon in the far south, closing the list of Simeon’s towns: “And Bethlebaoth, and Sharuhen; thirteen cities and their villages” (Jos 19:6). The name is taken to mean gracious dwelling, or abode of grace. It lay in the borderland toward the wilderness and the way to Egypt, a frontier town of the driest inheritance in Israel. That such a place should be called an abode of grace speaks well of the God who portioned it, for Simeon’s lot was hard ground — the parched Negeb, poor in water and beset by desert raiders. Yet grace can make its dwelling in a dry land, and the God who is gracious set His people even there. “The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth” (Exo 34:6): this is the character that names the town. Grace is not owed to the rich soil nor withheld from the poor; it dwells where God is pleased to set it, and turns a wilderness border into an abode of His favor. The believer, whose lot in this world may be barren enough, learns from Sharuhen that the abode of grace is wherever the gracious God has placed His own, and that His favor, not the fatness of the ground, makes any place a gracious dwelling.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of Simeon, in the south country of Judah; called Azem in the parallel Judah list. The name means “bone” and by extension “strength” or “might.”
biblical_def: Ezem is a city given to the tribe of Simeon in the south of Judah: “And Hazarshual, and Balah, and Azem” (Jos 19:3), where it is spelled Azem, and again in the roll of Judah’s southern towns (Jos 15:29). The name means bone, and from the firmness and framework of the bone it takes the sense of strength or might. In Scripture the bone is the emblem of the very substance and frame of a thing — Adam said of Eve, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Gen 2:23) — and of that inward strength which the LORD alone can uphold or break. The psalmist in his affliction cries that all his bones are out of joint; in his deliverance he says, “All my bones shall say, LORD, who is like unto thee?” (Psa 35:10). A town named Bone, or Strength, set in the frail and thirsty south of Simeon, quietly witnesses that the strength of God’s people is not their own frame but the LORD who is the strength of their life. It is He who keepeth all their bones, so that not one of them is broken — a word fulfilled in Christ upon the cross, of whom the Scripture said, “A bone of him shall not be broken.” The strength named at Ezem is finally the strength of the risen Lord, in whom the frailest saint is upheld.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of Simeon, afterward given to the priests as a Levitical city; the name means “spring” or “fountain,” and is not to be confounded with Ain the border-point of Canaan’s eastern line.
biblical_def: Ain is a city in the far south given to the tribe of Simeon: “Ain, Remmon, and Ether, and Ashan; four cities and their villages” (Jos 19:7). It was afterward set apart from Simeon’s portion to the priests as a Levitical city: “And Ain with her suburbs, and Juttah with her suburbs, and Bethshemesh with her suburbs” (Jos 21:16). The name means spring or fountain, for it was doubtless named from a source of living water in that thirsty land — and in the dry Negeb a spring was life itself. Water is one of the great Scriptural pictures of the grace and Spirit of God. The LORD is called “the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13), and He upbraids His people for forsaking Him, that fountain, to hew out broken cisterns that hold no water. A priestly town named Fountain preaches the calling of the ministry: the priests were set among the people to point them to the spring of living water, the LORD Himself, from whom alone the soul is refreshed. Christ cried, “If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink” (Joh 7:37), and promised that from the believer should flow rivers of living water. The fountain-town of Simeon, become a dwelling of the priests, is a small standing witness that God’s ministers exist to lead thirsty souls to Him who is the fountain of life.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of Reuben, east of Jordan, described as being “in the mount of the valley”; the name is taken to mean “splendor of the dawn” or “beauty of the morning.”
biblical_def: Zareth-shahar is a city in the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben, on the tableland east of Jordan, set with a rare touch of description: “And Kirjathaim, and Sibmah, and Zarethshahar in the mount of the valley” (Jos 13:19). The name is taken to mean splendor of the dawn, or beauty of the morning — a town, perhaps, that caught the first light upon its height above the valley. Of all the poetic names in the rolls of the inheritance, few so directly lift the reader’s eye to the great Scriptural picture of the dawn. The coming of God’s salvation is again and again likened to the breaking of the morning: “the dayspring from on high hath visited us” (Luk 1:78); “the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18). Christ Himself is “the bright and morning star” and the Sun of righteousness who arises with healing in His wings. A town named Splendor-of-the-Dawn, standing on its height to receive the first beams over the eastern hills, becomes a natural emblem of that hope: that after the long night of sin and death, the morning of redemption breaks, and the day of the Lord dawns upon His waiting people. The believer, set upon his watch, looks eastward for that splendor, and knows the night is far spent and the day at hand.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of the tribe of Gad, east of Jordan, near the border of the tableland; the name is taken to mean “pistachio nuts” or “hollows.”
biblical_def: Betonim is a border city in the inheritance of the tribe of Gad, east of Jordan: “And from Heshbon unto Ramathmizpeh, and Betonim; and from Mahanaim unto the border of Debir” (Jos 13:26). It is named only in the marking out of Gad’s bounds, and no story is attached to it. The name is taken to mean pistachio nuts, from a kind of tree that grew there, or hollows in the ground. Gad’s portion lay in the good pasture-land of Gilead, east of Jordan — a country the tribes of Reuben and Gad had asked for because they had much cattle and the land was fit for flocks. It was a lawful request granted, yet a solemn one, for those tribes chose their inheritance on the near side of Jordan, apart from the main body of Israel, and were the first to feel the brunt of the Syrian and Assyrian invasions and the first carried away captive. Betonim, a quiet border-town of that eastern land, stands in the record as one of the boundary-stones of Gad’s inheritance — a portion good and pleasant, yet exposed, and a reminder that the choice of a dwelling-place should weigh not only the fatness of the pasture but the nearness of one’s brethren and the safety of the fold under the hand of God.

corruption_summary: A city of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the sobering lesson of choosing an inheritance by the fatness of the pasture rather than nearness to God’s people.
corruption_paragraphs: Betonim faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth its setting carries answers the worldly wisdom that chooses its dwelling and its portion solely by profit and pleasant pasture, weighing not the safety of the soul nor the fellowship of the people of God.

etymology: A place in the land of Ammon, east of Jordan, to which Jephthah pursued and smote the Ammonites; the name means “meadow of vineyards” or “plain of the vineyards.”
biblical_def: Abel-keramim, the plain of the vineyards, is a place in the land of the children of Ammon, east of Jordan, marking the far point of Jephthah’s victory over them. When the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah and he went against Ammon, “he smote them from Aroer, even till thou come to Minnith, even twenty cities, and unto the plain of the vineyards, with a very great slaughter. Thus the children of Ammon were subdued before the children of Israel” (Jdg 11:33). The name meadow of vineyards paints a country of fruitful vine-land, and it was here, in the place of the vineyards, that God gave Israel a great deliverance from the oppressor who had vexed them eighteen years. Yet the victory of Jephthah is shadowed by his rash and unlawful vow, a warning woven into the same chapter. The deliverance was wholly of God, who raised up a judge and gave the enemy into his hand; the sorrow that followed was of man, who bound himself with a vow he ought never to have made. So the plain of the vineyards holds together both truths: that salvation is of the LORD, who subdues the enemies of His people, and that His servants must walk carefully, not ensnaring themselves with rash words, lest their very triumphs be mingled with needless grief.

corruption_paragraphs: Abel-keramim faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth its history carries answers both the pride that claims deliverance as its own doing and the presumption that binds itself with rash vows, thinking to move God by extravagant words.
